hidden-layer.name: Hidden layer
hidden-layer.definition: A layer whose activations are internal features rather than final predictions.
hidden-layer.explanation: A hidden layer receives inputs from an earlier layer and supplies transformed values to a later one. Its parameters are learned through gradients propagated from the loss. When a nonlinear activation lies between dense layers, the model can represent relationships that a single affine transformation cannot. Hidden does not mean inaccessible: during development we can inspect activations and gradients. The term only distinguishes these units from the provided inputs and requested outputs.

backpropagation.name: Backpropagation
backpropagation.definition: An efficient reverse application of the chain rule through a computation.
backpropagation.explanation: Backpropagation first evaluates a model and saves intermediate quantities, then sends derivatives from the scalar loss toward earlier parameters. Each operation multiplies an incoming derivative by its local derivative, while shared dependencies add contributions. The method computes the same analytical gradients one could derive symbolically, but reuses intermediate work. Parameters must remain at their forward-pass values until every gradient that depends on them has been computed.

nonlinearity.name: Nonlinearity
nonlinearity.definition: A function that prevents stacked affine layers from collapsing into one affine map.
nonlinearity.explanation: Sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU are common nonlinear activation functions. Without one between dense layers, multiplying and adding through several layers is algebraically equivalent to one weight matrix and bias, so depth adds no representational power. A nonlinearity changes both the forward values and the derivative passed backward. Its saturation or nondifferentiable points can affect optimization, which is why activation choice and initialization are connected.
